description: I am Isaac Akhigbe, a final year software engineering student. The purpose of this team is to develop Shuka, a decision‑support tool that uses NASA Earth observations along with local soil information, crop characteristics, and farmer priorities to help farmers explore rotation strategies that could strengthen soil health and adapt their farms to changing conditions
summary: Across Nigeria and five other African countries, the rainy season now starts later than it did in 1979, by more than 25 days in some places. A delay of just one week cuts crop yields by about 2%, and early false-start rains make it worse by pushing farmers to plant too soon (Kim Taveras, Bocconi University). We introduce Shuka, a platform that helps agricultural extension officers in northern Nigeria advise farmers on how, when and what to plant. It is a decision support tool that utilizes more than 25 years of NASA POWER climate data and turns it into a profile for each state. It also compares the crop rotation techniques used by farmers today with better alternatives, scored for water use, soil health, climate fit and income. Every option comes with a clear explanation of why it was suggested, the evidence, the benefits and the risks. This information is then sent to registered farmers as voice calls or SMS in the native languages of the farmers, which can work on any basic phone. This matters because most northern farmers rely on rain that is becoming less predictable, and Nigeria has roughly one extension worker for every 6,466 farm families, so good advice rarely reaches them in time.
details:
What exactly does it do?

Shuka is a decision support tool for crop planning that serves extension officers and the farmers they advise. Specifically,

  1. It shows an interactive web dashboard with a map of 19 northern states plus FCT, where selecting a state opens a climate profile computed from NASA POWER data (rain reliability, false onset rate, safe planting date, season length, heat stress days and root-zone soil wetness)
  2. It gives a rotation planner that takes three inputs from the extension officer, the state being advised, the rotation most farmers there use today (e.g. maize after maize, or sorghum with cowpea every year), and the farmers' top priority (save water, improve soil, earn more or lower risk). These inputs set the weights in Shuka's scoring engine, so the same climate data gives different advice for different farmer needs
  3. It shows at least three rotations compared side by side, including current practice, each with a score, why it was suggested, the evidence, benefits, risks and what a local expert should check
  4. It calculates a safe planting window for each state, based on 25 years of rainfall onset dates. A false onset warning tells farmers to wait when early rains are likely to be followed by a dry spell
  5. It delivers the advice straight to registered farmers as voice calls in their local language, and by SMS for rain warnings. Both work on any basic phone with no internet, smartphone or app needed, and voice calls reach farmers who cannot read

How does it work?

  1. Climate Data Analysis: Shuka keeps the last 25 years of daily NASA POWER data (rainfall, max temperature and root-zone soil wetness) for each state, refreshed daily during the planting season and monthly otherwise. From this, the backend builds a climate profile per state, covering rain reliability, onset date, false onset rate, season length, heat stress days and soil wetness.
  2. Crop and Rotation Library: A library of crops grown in northern Nigeria, each with its water needs, days to maturity, drought and heat tolerance, nitrogen fixing and market value, plus the common rotations farmers in the north use today. New crops and rotations can be added without changing the engine.
  3. Scoring Engine: Each rotation is scored against the state’s NASA-derived climate profile for water use, soil health, climate fit and income, weighted by what the farmers need most. Every score comes with a plain explanation of why it was suggested, the evidence, the benefits and the risks.
  4. Simplified Advice for Farmers: AI rewrites the engine’s results as a plain-language briefing with answers to likely farmer questions. It only rewords facts from Shuka’s NASA analysis, and the extension officer approves every briefing.
  5. Delivery: With one click, the officer sends the advice to every registered farmer in the state as voice calls and SMS in the farmer’s own language, including false rain warnings, on any basic phone with no internet.

What benefits does it have?

  1. Stronger Extension Services: With one extension worker for about every 6,466 farm families, officers can’t reach most farmers in person. Shuka lets one officer send the same reliable, data-backed advice to thousands of farmers in minutes, which frees their time for the farmers who need face-to-face help.
  2. Food Security and Farmer Income: Fewer failed plantings mean bigger harvests across the north, which can help ease pressure on food supply and prices. Farmers waste less seed, labour and fertiliser on failed plantings and earn more from better yields, and legume rotations cut fertiliser costs further.
  3. Inclusion: Shuka works on any basic phone with no internet, smartphone or app, and delivers advice in the farmer’s own language. Voice calls also reach farmers who can’t read. This matters most for women farmers, since research shows plots managed by women suffer significantly larger yield losses when the rains come late.
  4. Environmental and Climate Resilience: Rotating cereals with legumes like cowpea and groundnut puts nitrogen back into the soil, which keeps it healthy and cuts the need for chemical fertiliser. Matching crops to the rainfall saves water. As the seasons keep shifting, advice is based on recent NASA data instead of old planting calendars, so farmers can adapt year by year.

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, we aim to pilot Shuka in the 2027 rainy season with one northern state's Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) and its extension officers. We'll measure the results by comparing failed plantings and yields between farmers who received Shuka's advice and those who didn't. We also plan to partner with the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet), so Shuka's false rain warnings line up with the official onset forecasts farmers already hear about.

In the long term, we want Shuka to strengthen food security, soil health and farmer incomes across Nigeria. We plan to add more local languages and an AI voice agent that farmers can talk to and ask questions by phone. We’ll also bring in more NASA data, such as GPM IMERG rainfall and SMAP soil moisture, for finer advice at the local government level. And farmers will be able to register themselves from any phone through a USSD short code. Beyond the north, we aim to expand to the southern states and then to other West African countries that share the same rain belt.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend. Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet (interactive map) with Esri map tiles (light grey and satellite)
  • Backend. Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn, SQLite database, PBKDF2 password hashing for officer sign-in
  • Data. NASA POWER daily point API
  • AI. Large language model API for farmer-ready messages
  • Voice and SMS. Twilio (voice calls and SMS, with a TwiML Bin to play the audio), ElevenLabs (local-language voice recordings)
  • Hosting and tools. Vercel (frontend), Render (backend), Git, GitHub, jsDelivr (audio files)
